# 宗教·神话·灵性 {.unnumbered}



> 本主题共 8 篇语境短文。每篇把一批旧词织进一个场景；目标词**加粗**，展开"本篇生词"可遮释义自测。



### At the Threshold of the Sacred

The old **pagan** village had no **bible**, no **papal** authority, no **sect** to claim it — only a moss-covered **altar** at the forest's edge where every harvest moon the elders placed a clay **joss** figure as an offering. A wandering **guru** arrived one autumn, sat cross-legged on a **pew** dragged out from a half-ruined chapel, and began recounting the **myth** of **Horus** — the falcon-headed god whose eye, torn away and restored, became the symbol of healing across the ancient world. Children gathered, wide-eyed, half-believing the stranger had placed a **hex** on the air itself, for his words seemed to shimmer.

He spoke of **karma**, of how every act coils back upon the actor the way smoke circles before it rises; of **Amor** and **Cupid** — the same longing rendered in two tongues; of **Deus**, the root-word that branched into a dozen divine names across a dozen faiths. He read from **Amos** and from **Ezra**, two voices out of the same ancient hunger, and when he chanted their verses they sounded almost like **hymns**. Two **nuns** who had wandered down from the hillside monastery stood at the back, listening without interrupting, their faces open.

By nightfall the mood had darkened pleasantly. Someone lit incense near the **tomb** of the village founder, its carved face worn smooth by rain and decades of touch. Talk turned to the **demon** that local legend said haunted the crossroads, and to the **devil**-bargains folklore warned against. A young skeptic challenged the guru's **dogma** outright, calling the whole evening a **cult** gathering dressed in respectability. The guru smiled — the **zen** kind, maddening in its calm — and gestured toward the **ephod** he wore, a narrow linen vestment draped across his shoulders, saying only that every cloth, every **vow**, every murmured **hymn** is finally an attempt to touch what the word **piety** has always meant: the ache to be faithful to something larger than oneself. The skeptic sat back down. Outside, **Amor** shot no arrows; the night needed none. The **vows** people carried inwardly were already doing their work.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}

### The Shrine at the Edge of the World

The old **curate** arrived at the hilltop **parish** just before dawn, his robes smelling of incense from the **censer** he had swung through the night vigil. He was a **devout** man — not in any **pious**, performative sense, but quietly so, shaped by decades of **rites** that had worn smooth grooves into his days. The **deacon** who met him at the door pressed a worn **tarot** card into his palm — a relic left by some wanderer — and said nothing. Inside, above the altar, a painted **Apollo** gazed down with that serene, almost **deific** calm that old craftsmen gave to gods they still half-believed in.

The **pastor** lit the morning candles and began to chant a **psalm**, low and unhurried, the syllables rising like smoke. Someone had chalked a **mantra** on the stone floor, letters overlapping the chalk outline of an older, stranger symbol — something **occult**, pre-Christian, the kind of mark that made scholars argue about **dharma** and **divine** will in the same breath. The **Elohim**, **Isaiah** insisted in the scripture pinned to the lectern, tolerated no **fetish**, no carved **goblin** standing in for the holy. And yet here they all were, layered: the **kosher** prohibition on one wall, a notice about the upcoming **Purim** celebration on another, and beside it a hand-lettered flyer for a **fiesta** the following weekend.

The curate was due to **ordain** a young man that afternoon — to **anoint** his head with oil and speak the words that would **hallow** him, set him apart, send him into a world that included, somewhere in its shadows, every name for darkness ever coined: **DIABLO** in one tongue, **satan** in another, a **goblin** king in a third. **Heaven**, the curate thought, is less a place than a direction — the way you face when you decide what to **hallow** and what to refuse. He folded the tarot card into his pocket, nodded to **Elijah**'s portrait on the wall, and went to prepare.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}

### Shadows of the Sacred: From **Temple** to **Zodiac**

In the oldest cities, a **priest** would climb the steps of the **temple** at dawn, where the scent of incense rose toward ceilings painted with every sign of the **zodiac**. The **sacred** space was not merely stone; it was a threshold between the mortal and the divine. Painted **cherubs** hovered above the altar, and on certain feast days the congregation would gather to hear a **sermon** delivered from the **pulpit**, its timber worn smooth by generations of gripping hands. Before the **ritual** began, **devotee**s spent the previous night **fasting**, seeking purity before they **invoked** the name of their god. An **Aaronic** blessing would then be chanted — words tracing their lineage back to the first **apostle**s who carried the faith beyond their homeland.

Yet belief rarely travels without fracture. A **schism** tore the community in two when a **gnostic** teacher arrived, whispering that hidden knowledge — not public ceremony — was the only path to truth. The elders declared him a **heretic**, but his followers multiplied. Among them was an **ascetic** who survived on dried figs and water, and an **acolyte** who had once dreamed of becoming a **messiah** figure himself. The conflict played out with the quiet menace of **alchemy**: doctrines transformed, base arguments transmuted into creeds. **Judaism**, Christianity, and older mystery traditions all left traces in the dispute, each side claiming its own lineage of **martyrs** who had died rather than **repent**.

It was a wandering **masonic** lodge that finally offered neutral ground. In their hall, old grievances were set aside long enough for both factions to attend the **funeral** of the community's founder together. Standing at the graveside, the surviving priest allowed himself to be **bewitched** — not by magic, but by grief and the strange beauty of shared loss. He opened the **Psalms** to a passage about redemption, his voice steadying as he read. Perhaps, he thought, the only way to **redeem** the community was not to win the argument but to **baptism**-wash the wound clean and begin again. Whether that was wisdom or wishful thinking, no one at the **shrine** that day could say.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}

### The Seeker Who Crossed Every Threshold

In the ancient temple district, where the smell of incense never quite left the stone, a young scholar arrived carrying only a water-skin and the **Biblical** texts his mother had pressed into his hands at parting. He had been **baptized** as an infant in a village so small it had no name on any map, **christened** with the name **Emmanuel** — *God with us* — though by now he doubted whether any god was with anyone at all. His tutors back home would have called him an **apostate**, a word that landed like a stone in still water; his own heart preferred the quieter label of **agnostic**. He simply did not know.

The first temple he entered was consecrated to **Mithras**, the bull-slaying god of soldiers and oaths. A fresco showed the deity surrounded by a **trinity** of torchbearers, their faces worn to soft smears by centuries of lamp-smoke. The **cardinal** directions were marked in red ochre on the floor. A lone **celibate** priest — bound by vow to neither wife nor wine — sat in the inner **sanctum**, copying the book of **Numbers** by hand onto stretched hide. The scholar watched the priest's steady fingers and felt, briefly, the appeal of a life so narrowed that every choice had already been made.

Outside, the market pressed against the temple walls. A hawker sold amulets against **Satanic** influence; a pamphleteer denounced the old gods as **profane** idols; a painter was finishing a mural of a **phoenix** rising from a pyre, its wings the color of embers. The scholar paused before it. He had read that the bird never truly died — it was the burning itself that was the point. Nearby, in the **cemetery** at the edge of the district, the names of the city's **gentiles** were carved in a script he could not read, their **secular** lives reduced to dates and the occasional flower cut in stone.

That evening a wandering teacher — one of those itinerant figures the locals half-reverently called an **apostle** of the mountain path — led a small group in meditation. He spoke of **nirvana** not as a reward but as the simple exhaustion of craving, the way a lamp goes dark not because someone blows it out but because the oil is gone. He spoke of **samadhi**, the still point where the meditator and the object of meditation collapse into one, where even the **specter** of self fades. The scholar tried to follow and instead watched a moth navigate the lantern flame, terrified and drawn at once.

Later a **spectre** of doubt moved through him — the old kind, the kind that **nemesis** sends not as punishment but as education. He had seen a bishop propose to **canonize** a local healer; he had watched an **Epiphany** procession in which children carried candles through fog, their faces ghostly as **phantoms**; he had sat beside a man who claimed a shaman had **exorcised** a grief from his chest the way one removes a splinter. The world, he decided, was not waiting to be classified. It was **Proteus** — slipping through every grip, wearing every shape, refusing to hold still long enough to be pinned. The right response was not certainty. The right response was to **enshrine** the question itself, to carry it carefully, the way one carries a flame.

He slept under the portico and dreamed of the **phoenix** again.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}

### A Flame Kept Burning — Across Temples, Heresies, and Dreams

In a **lamasery** tucked high in the frost-bitten peaks, the monks rose before dawn to chant verses from **Proverbs** — words they believed could **sanctify** the ordinary act of breathing. The head lama, a figure of quiet **sanctity**, moved through the **hieratic** rituals with hands so steady they seemed carved from the mountain itself. Pilgrims who made the climb spoke of reaching a kind of **paradise** — not the gilded afterlife promised elsewhere, but a stillness in the chest that felt **hallowed**, as though the air itself had been set apart.

Down in the valley, the story grew more tangled. A **Lutheran** minister and a wandering **alchemist** argued by firelight: the minister insisted that **atonement** was the axis on which all meaning turned, quoting **Immanuel** as proof that the divine had once walked in dust and sweat; the alchemist countered with **solarism**, tracing every savior myth back to the arc of the sun. A young **ordinand** listened from the shadows, uncertain which tradition he was preparing to serve. Nearby, a woman who could **soothsay** unrolled a star chart — her **astrology** was dismissed as superstition by the **apostolic** elder, who muttered warnings about **idolatry** and the **heresies** that rot a congregation from within. Yet the elder himself kept, locked in his trunk, a forbidden **theogony** — a **reverend** old manuscript tracing the births and wars of gods far older than his own.

Night deepened, and the **Arthurian** tapestry on the wall stirred in the draft: **unicorns** rearing beside a wounded king, **immortal** knights who refused to fall. Someone whispered that the hall was cursed — that **succubae** and the lone **succubus** who led them rose from **Tartarus** to feed on faith that had grown vain. **Augustine** had warned against exactly this: the soul that mistakes its own hunger for **prophecy**, that calls private longing an **apostolic** vision. But the night was long, and every **atheistic** doubt dissolved a little in the firelight — leaving only the oldest question, unanswerable and unextinguished, floating above the embers like smoke.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}

### Shadows of the Sacred

In the great **cathedral** whose stones had stood since the first **Christian** missionaries arrived, a **Methodist** preacher once climbed the pulpit and declared that all rival traditions were **heretical** — words the **episcopal** council would later rule a **blasphemy** against the unity of the faith. The **canonical** texts, they insisted, left no room for such **Manichean** divisions between light and absolute darkness. Among the pews sat a quiet scholar of **Levitical** law, his worn copy of **Leviticus** open beside him, silently recounting how even the **Sadducees** of ancient Jerusalem had quarrelled over resurrection — the same hope that drove every **sacrament** performed in this very hall.

Outside the cathedral walls, other seekers gathered in the shadow of a nearby **monastery**, trading **esoterica** that the church would sooner burn than canonise. An **occultist** versed in the lore of a **freemason** lodge murmured to his companion about **Kundalini** energy rising through the spine — a path to inner **salvation** he preferred to any **purgatory** of prescribed ritual. The companion, a woman of **confucian** disposition who had studied the sayings of **Confucius** in Nanjing before sailing west, listened without judgment; she had long grown accustomed to the **recusancy** of those who refused the **synagogue** and the nave alike, choosing instead the unmarked **sanctuary** of wild hills at dawn. Somewhere beneath the roots of that hill, legend promised, lay **Excalibur**, a sword whose power was beyond **the devil** himself to corrupt — though the **occultism** peddled around its myth had long since consigned several true believers to **perdition**.

Only the old woman in the corner went on whispering the **Hail Mary**, her lips moving in their familiar rhythm, trusting that something — however named, however carved in stone or legend — would, in its own hour, **resurrect** the world.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}

### Between the Living and the Gone

At the edge of the village, beneath a yew older than memory, stood a weathered **tombstone** carved with a single candle flame — the emblem of a local **Unitarian** congregation that had quietly practiced its faith for two centuries. Tradition held that the flame was lit by **Zoroaster** himself, a legend almost certainly **apocryphal**, yet repeated with the solemn warmth of something believed.

Every autumn, on **Michaelmas**, the priest would lead a procession past the stone to the chapel, where the **liturgical** chant of the **Benedictus** rose into the rafters. The rite was ancient: incense, candle-wax, and the low drone of the **evangelical** choir. Somewhere in the archive, a manuscript described a **coronation** of abbots performed on this same ground — a **consecrated** hill where **immolation** of grain and oil had once sealed a covenant between the community and whatever force governed rain and harvest. A **Melchizedek** figure, priest-king and stranger, was said to have presided. Whether that story was scripture or **soothsaying** no scholar had settled.

Inside the chapel, a lay **evangelist** taught a class on **monotheism**, tracing the long argument against the older **priesthood** of many gods. He had spent a decade studying **asceticism** and its rivals — the Protestant suspicion of mortification, the Quaker trust in inner light, the exotic circuits of **scientology**, the quiet discipline of **reincarnate** tradition in the East. He spoke of **redemption** and **deliverance** as if they were doors you could choose to open, of **veneration** as a posture of the whole body, not merely the mind. Behind him, through a small arch, the **tabernacle** gleamed in candlelight.

When the rector took the podium to **pontificate** on the end of days — drawing on **apocalyptic** texts with the confidence of someone who had read them all — his **benediction** rolled through the hall like low thunder. Outside, the sky had turned that particular violet that always made people reach for **apocalypse** as the only word large enough. The stained glass cast broken light across the floor. **Providence**, someone whispered, though no one was sure what they meant by it. The **crucifixion** panel glowed deepest red. The **deliverance** panel, pale gold.

In the courtyard afterward, two children traced the letters on the old **tombstone** with their fingers, sounding out a name nobody living could now remember.

### A Scholar's Vigil at the Edge of the Sacred

In the high-vaulted library of an old seminary, Brother Edmund sat hunched over texts that spanned every **ecclesiastical** tradition he could name. His dissertation was a **theological** survey of how ancient peoples moved from polytheism toward **monotheistic** faith — a journey mapped not through the **crystal ball** of prophecy but through patient reading. He belonged to no single **denomination**, though he had been raised **Episcopalian** and still felt the quiet pull of that ordered liturgy. On the shelf beside him stood a jar of **frankincense**, its resin scenting the cold air and carrying his thoughts toward something older than argument.

Downstairs, the Sunday **congregation** gathered under the ministry of a visiting **televangelist** whose flair for **evangelicalism** made the older deacons uneasy. The man's theology leaned hard **Trinitarian**, invoking the threefold name at every turn, and rumor held that his predecessor had been threatened with **excommunicate**d status after feuding with the bishop. Edmund found such spectacle tiresome. He preferred the quieter logic of **transcendentalism**, the **transcendentalist** conviction that the divine shone directly through conscience and nature — no mediator required. He kept a dog-eared copy of the **Song of Solomon** open on the lectern, its aching imagery far more alive to him than any broadcast sermon.

Outside, a procession marked the feast of **resurrection**, candles tracing a slow orbit around the churchyard. Edmund watched from his window and thought about **transmigration** — how certain Eastern traditions imagined the soul cycling through lives the way seasons cycle through a year, each existence a step toward something **paradisiacal**. Against such vast cosmologies, the West's fear of **superstition** could look like a failure of imagination. Yet he also understood **enshrinement**: the human need to fix a sacred thing in stone and ritual, to make the ineffable endure. He recalled a mosaic of **Pontius Pilate** in a Ravenna chapel — the governor's hands forever mid-wash, guilt crystallized into gold tessera.

He returned to his notes. The modern church still wrestled with questions that **theological** councils had debated for centuries, questions no **crystal ball** could settle: how belief travels, what it costs to belong, and whether grace could survive **transmigration** from one age's language into the next. From somewhere below, a choir rose through the floorboards — a hymn that closed, as he knew it would, *with Love Divine.*
